title: Deported in 1999, Brooklyn Man Can Still Seek Sale of Home Bought in 1985, Court Rules
excerpt: New York's Appellate Division held that because Clyde Nelson's 2007 divorce never disposed of the Brooklyn house, his ownership share survived — and his former wife cannot use the divorce to block his partition claim.
body:
• A New York appeals court ruled on November 18 that Clyde Nelson — removed from the United States in 1999 and never returned — can pursue the forced sale of the Brooklyn home he co-owns with his former wife.
  • The couple's 2007 divorce never disposed of the house, so their ownership converted from a tenancy by the entirety to a tenancy in common, and his share survived the divorce.
  • The ruling affirms a 2022 lower-court order; it does not order a sale or set either side's share of any proceeds — the partition case continues.
  • For diaspora readers: deportation did not erase a name on a deed, and a divorce that skips a property leaves ownership — and disputes — alive for decades.

A man who was removed from the United States 27 years ago has won the right to seek the sale of the Brooklyn home he still co-owns with his former wife. On November 18, the Appellate Division of the New York Supreme Court, Second Department, ruled in Nelson v. Nelson that Clyde Nelson can proceed with his partition action against Verna Nelson, affirming a lower court's order, according to the court's decision as reported by LAWS.com and the Times of India.

A house, a removal and a divorce that skipped the property

Clyde and Verna Nelson married in 1977. They bought the Brooklyn property in 1985, with title held in Clyde's name alone; in 1988 the title was changed to include both spouses. Verna has been in sole possession of the home since about 1995. Clyde was removed from the United States in 1999 and has not returned since.

In 2007, a judgment of divorce was entered against Clyde by default. Critically, that judgment did not address the couple's marital property: as the appeals court quoted, "the judgment of divorce did not dispose of any marital property and the complaint expressly stated that equitable distribution of marital property was not being sought." In 2019, Clyde sued for partition — the legal process by which a co-owner asks a court to divide jointly owned property or order its sale — seeking to sell the house and divide the proceeds. Verna moved to block the claim, arguing it should have been raised in the divorce and was barred by the doctrines of res judicata and collateral estoppel.

What the court held

The Supreme Court in Kings County sided with Clyde in an order dated September 15, 2022, denying Verna's motion and granting his cross-motion confirming his right to seek partition. The Second Department — Justices Valerie Brathwaite Nelson, Deborah A. Dowling, Janice A. Taylor and Laurence L. Love — has now affirmed that order, with costs.

The reasoning turns on what the divorce did and did not do. Because the judgment never disposed of the house, it "did not extinguish the plaintiff's ownership interest in the property or otherwise affect the parties' rights with respect to the subject property," the court wrote. The divorce did change the form of ownership: a married couple's tenancy by the entirety became a tenancy in common, under which each former spouse holds an independent share — and a tenant in common may sue for partition. Verna's res judicata and collateral estoppel arguments failed because the property question had never actually been decided.

What it does and does not mean

The ruling does not sell the house, and it does not decide how any proceeds would be split; it confirms that Clyde's partition case can continue. For immigrant families, the case carries two practical lessons that lawyers see repeatedly. First, removal from the United States does not by itself cancel property rights recorded on a deed. Second, a divorce — especially a default divorce obtained while one spouse is abroad — that never mentions a property leaves that property in legal limbo, owned by both ex-spouses until a court deals with it, however many years later.
